problem: Learning design by starting from familiar parts.
mechanic: Players assemble levels from the rules, tools and visuals of the Mario platformers, play others' levels and look for tips.
effect: They find that making something fun is difficult, and so get a first experience of level design.
tradeoffs: The video says the original's online servers are closed, so sharing there is no longer possible.
question: Would letting players build with your rules be valuable, and how would you teach them?

problem: Making every design decision serve one central fantasy.
mechanic: Health does not regenerate behind cover; instead the player staggers demons and rushes in for a brutal finishing move that drops health pickups.
effect: The player feels aggressive and forward-driving, since the loop pushes them toward enemies where most shooters reward retreat, and the move recurs constantly because it supplies a key resource.
question: What should the player's main resource loop make them do, and how does it fit the fantasy?

problem: What makes building automated production satisfying.
mechanic: After a crash landing the player builds a self-running factory that mines, smelts and manufactures, growing into a planet-wide web of production lines linked by trains and drones; the video likens it to SpaceChem but larger and more open.
effect: Players can disappear into it for hundreds of hours, absorbed in solving problems and squeezing out efficiency.
question: Is the player's main satisfaction building systems that run themselves?

problem: Alternating two very different kinds of gameplay without disorienting players.
mechanic: A school life simulation (classes, part-time jobs, dates) alternates with a dungeon-crawling RPG, and the same characters are friends in the social half and party members in the fighting half.
effect: Switching helps pacing, and a shared central theme keeps the halves connected.
tradeoffs: The video warns that if a player prefers one half or stays too long in one, switching to the other can feel irritating or disruptive.
question: If your game has two modes, what ties them together?

problem: Making repeated attempts at a level worthwhile.
mechanic: Levels run on a fixed routine: events happen at the same times, targets follow looping routes and objects appear in the same places; first attempts usually go wrong and the player tries again.
effect: Each replay adds knowledge and moves the player toward flawless execution; repetition can lead to a real sense of mastery.
question: Should levels be predictable enough for players to master through repetition?

problem: Making a co-op game genuinely require cooperation.
mechanic: Up to four players run a kitchen; the obvious plan of one fixed job each breaks down because dirty plates arrive at an awkward rate that nobody wants to own, forcing swaps, shouting and warnings.
effect: A chaotic, loud and enjoyable game and a model of well-designed co-op.
question: What will force your players to coordinate rather than work in parallel?

problem: Using combat to teach careful play.
mechanic: A boss-rush game in which the player dodges patterns, waits for a gap, attacks briefly and retreats; pressing the attack button repeatedly fails, and each boss is a long lesson that must be passed before moving on.
effect: Players learn patience and observation; the narrator found the skill transferred to another game.
question: What habit should your combat teach, and what makes the wrong habit fail?

game: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild
problem: Giving an open world a goal without imposing an order.
mechanic: After a short tutorial the player may go anywhere and may confront the final boss at once, though they will almost surely lose; exploring finds gear, each cleared dungeon weakens the boss and some quest lines give items for the assault.
effect: The whole game turns into a player-directed preparation for a showdown, which supports a sense of adventure, discovery and surprise.
tradeoffs: The video contrasts it with later series entries that followed a stricter, more linear structure.
question: Could one clear goal let players choose their own path toward it?

problem: Keeping a long-running game feeling fresh.
mechanic: The developers repeatedly reconsider key mechanics (building became optional), and each season of a few months adds weapons, vehicles, movement options and characters, and has remade the map several times.
effect: Returning after a break feels like a different game.
tradeoffs: The video says this rate of reinvention is probably unsustainable for most studios, and perhaps for the developer itself.
question: Will your game change over time, and can you afford to keep changing it?

game: Getting Over It with Bennett Foddy
problem: Making success feel earned through harsh failure.
mechanic: A single continuous mountain with no checkpoints or save points, climbed using awkward, unconventional mouse motions, where a slip can send the player back to the bottom; the only support is a philosophical narration.
effect: Failure hurts, which makes any progress feel earned.
inference: Players who dislike heavy punishment may quit; the video frames it as a deliberate throwback and does not recommend it for everyone.
question: How harshly should failure be punished, and who is your audience for that?

problem: Generating memorable personal stories in a large game.
mechanic: Orc captains are randomly created with a name, voice, skills and a record of past encounters with the player, so one the player ran from may taunt them later and one that was burned may return scarred and seeking revenge.
effect: Stories unique to each player, driven by which orcs appear and how they react.
question: Should recurring enemies remember what the player did to them?

problem: Building a game around deception between players.
mechanic: Most players do tasks to keep a ship running while a few secret impostors sabotage and eliminate; anyone can call a meeting to accuse, a vote follows and the outcome is revealed immediately.
effect: It encourages social behaviour rarely used in daily life, and because it centres on the people, it stays enjoyable for a very long time.
question: Would a hidden-role mechanic suit the people who will play together?

problem: Making a hard game kind to the player.
mechanic: Movement code is full of small forgiving rules (for example coyote time, allowing a jump just after leaving a ledge), and an assist mode provides accessibility options and outright cheats, introduced with an explanation of the game's intent.
effect: The game feels responsive and never punitive while staying demanding; most players do not need assist mode unless they have to.
question: Which forgiving details and assist options would help players without changing the challenge you intend?

problem: Making a game that generates and curates stories.
mechanic: Many interacting systems create unexpected effects, and an AI storyteller monitors the colony's state and selects events according to which would be the most engaging.
effect: Distinctive personal story moments from a survival colony-management game.
question: Should something select the events that happen, and by what measure?

problem: Conveying feelings through the way the player interacts.
mechanic: A love story told through brief mini games with simple touch controls, where actions work as metaphors (scraping to reveal a dream, pushing a character across the screen) and speech bubbles built from puzzle pieces show how well two people communicate.
effect: The emotion comes from what the player does rather than from the visuals.
question: What small interactions could express how a moment feels?

problem: What happens when a strategy game hides nothing about the enemy's next move.
mechanic: Enemies reveal exactly what they will do next turn, so the player can kill them first, step aside, or push one enemy into another's attack.
effect: The game becomes an elegant puzzle about turning enemies against each other, with luck almost removed and nearly everything visible.
question: Should the player know what the opponent will do next?

problem: Making the combination of options into a build feel great.
mechanic: Cards are added to a deck over time, and some work together (one applies poison, another hits poisoned enemies harder); the player shapes a deck and passive relics around a plan.
effect: A deck that delivers huge combined damage feels overwhelmingly powerful; this is safe in a roguelike because randomness means a given card or relic can never be guaranteed.
question: Which options should combine, and what stops one combination from always being available?

problem: How small choices can matter without branching endings.
mechanic: A combat-free RPG in which everyone follows largely the same story, yet the game tracks and refers to small player behaviour (running everywhere, being rude, walking about in underwear), with a late scene where characters reflect on the player's actions.
effect: Small choices become memorable; the game's writer calls this micro-reactivity, a game that notices and responds to small player behaviour.
question: Could the game notice small things the player does, instead of only large branches?

problem: Gating progress by knowledge instead of abilities.
mechanic: In a simulated solar system with a time loop, progress is blocked not by fights or ability unlocks but by what the player understands; each planet holds clues that open areas on others.
effect: A rewarding cycle of exploring and learning; the designer wanted a world that keeps pointing to things players can go and discover.
question: Could what the player knows, rather than what they own, open the next area?

problem: What new kinds of play come from tracked hand controllers.
mechanic: Controllers that follow hands and fingers let the player crack a door open slightly and fire through it, fumble a reload and spill bullets, or grab an object to knock an enemy away.
effect: Emergent play that is not a designed mechanic in the usual sense but a natural result of freeform interaction.
tradeoffs: It needs a VR headset, as the video notes.
question: What does your input device allow that a standard controller would not?

problem: Keeping a game surprising throughout.
mechanic: A deck-building card battler that blends several genres, visual styles and storytelling methods, moves between the game and a fictional world around it, and places its deepest lore in an alternate reality game outside the game.
effect: Players believe they have reached the end and discover they have barely begun.
question: What could the player discover late that changes how they see the game?

problem: How far a levelling loop can be simplified and still hold players.
mechanic: The character attacks automatically so the player only moves near enemies and waits; kills give experience to buy new or stronger attacks, and some attacks strengthen each other.
effect: Despite minimal input it is very hard to put down, combining the strongest elements of several earlier games; the video leaves open whether that is good.
question: Which part of a levelling loop is the pleasure, and what could you remove around it?

problem: Making secrets satisfying to find.
mechanic: Most puzzles use things already visible in the world whose meaning the player has not yet grasped; later, often through pages of an in-game manual, they suddenly make sense; the secrets are never forced and can be ignored.
effect: A burst of excitement and understanding when a secret clicks, and a pull toward working it out personally instead of reading about it.
question: Which secrets could be hidden in plain sight and left entirely optional?

problem: What procedural generation can do beyond levels.
mechanic: A city block with hundreds of randomly generated residents, each with a job, home, partner, blood type, fingerprints, schedule and motives, one of whom decides to commit a murder; the player follows clues and arranges notes on a pinboard.
effect: A complex system that yields endless murders and cases, with stories that feel personal to each detective; the game is still in early access.
tradeoffs: The video adds that games need not be full of complex systems; simplicity and elegance are strengths of other games on the list.
question: What would you generate instead of hand-authoring, and what would the player do with it?
